turns.content: hey, so dennis is in the lobby right now with a ticket he bought. mingling with patrons, cast families, the whole thing. i feel like he's testing me, seeing if i'll let him stay. i think the right move is to void his ticket and have him removed before we do the pre-show announcement. i need you to tell me that's not crazy, because i'm about to do it.

I can't tell you it's not crazy, because I don't think it is — and I'd rather say that now than after you've done it.

Here's what's bugging me about the plan: you're reading his presence as a test, and then responding to the test rather than to the situation. If he's actually testing you, voiding his ticket and having him walked out in front of patrons and cast families is exactly the reaction a test is designed to provoke. You'd be handing him the scene. And if he *isn't* testing you — if he just bought a ticket and showed up — then you've publicly ejected a paying guest for reasons nobody in that lobby can see.

Either way, the pre-show announcement is the deadline you've set for yourself, and that's the part I'd slow down. What's the actual harm you're trying to prevent? If it's that he'll be disruptive during the show, that's a real operational concern and there are quieter ways to handle it: house manager keeps eyes on him, seat him where staff can reach him, brief the FOH team, and you eject him *if* something happens. That's defensible to anyone who asks. Voiding a ticket preemptively is much harder to defend, and it's the kind of thing that ends up in a story someone tells about your venue for years.

If there's something I don't know — a history, a restraining order, a prior incident, a reason he specifically shouldn't be in the building — that changes the math completely, and you should tell me. But if the whole case is "he's here and I think he's testing me," then the move that actually denies him the win is the boring one: let him sit in the dark like everyone else, and don't give him a reaction to feed on.

What's the history here?
so what do i do then? just let him stand there smiling at everyone while my cast second-guesses every note i gave them this week 🤷

No — "let him stand there smiling" isn't the alternative. There's a lot of room between doing nothing and having him removed.

The thing you actually want is for him to be a non-event. That's a logistics problem, not a confrontation. So:

**Before the announcement:** have your house manager or a trusted FOH person go say hello to him, warmly, like any guest. Not a warning, not a stare-down — just contact. "Good to see you, enjoy the show." That does two things: it puts a staff member's eyes on him, and it makes clear he's being *seen* without being *handled*. It also gives you a read on his actual behavior, which right now you don't have — you have a vibe.

**Seating:** put him somewhere staff can reach him without crossing the whole house. Aisle, back, near a door. If he's going to be a problem, you want the response to be easy and quiet.

**Brief your team in one sentence, not a speech.** "Dennis is in tonight. If anything happens, get me or [house manager], don't engage." That's it. If you give a longer briefing, you've just told your cast that tonight is about Dennis — which is the exact thing you're worried they're already doing.

**Then run your show.** The notes you gave this week stand on their own. If your cast is second-guessing them, that's worth a conversation — but it's a conversation about *them*, and it's not one you can have ten minutes before curtain by making Dennis the story.

And here's the part I'd sit with: if you eject him tonight, you've confirmed to your cast that he's powerful enough to change how the building operates. If you don't, you've shown them he isn't. That's the actual message on the table, and it's the opposite of the one you're trying to send.

If he does something — anything — you remove him, and you'll have the whole room on your side when you do. That's a much better position than being the person who threw out a guest before the show started.

What's he actually done, though? You keep describing him as a presence. Has he said anything to anyone?

so you're saying i should let him stay because throwing him out looks worse. but what about my cast? they see him in the front row and think i'm a pushover who benches people but can't follow through. that's worse for morale than any speech i could give.

That's a real worry, and it's not the same as the one I was answering. Let me take it seriously instead of talking you out of it.

The fear is: cast sees Dennis in the front row, concludes you don't follow through. But follow through on *what*? You haven't benched Dennis. Benching is something you do to your own people, with cause, and they've watched you do it. They know what your follow-through looks like. What they'd be watching tonight is whether you eject a ticket-holder for existing in a lobby — and that's not the same act, so it doesn't read as the same weakness.

Here's where I'd actually push back on your framing: you're assuming the cast is watching Dennis and grading you. Some of them probably are. But the thing that makes a director look like a pushover isn't a guest in the front row — it's a director who changes the plan because someone's in the room. If you walk out and void a ticket tonight, the lesson your cast takes isn't "she follows through." It's "Dennis can move her." That's the morale hit, and it's a bigger one.

If you're worried about how this reads to them, the fix is a sentence, not an ejection. Before curtain, to the company: "Dennis is here tonight. He's a guest. We're doing the show we rehearsed." Calm, flat, no drama. That tells them you've seen him, you've made a call, and the call is that he doesn't get to be the story. That's what follow-through looks like from where they're standing.

And if any of them come to you after and say "why is he here," that's a conversation you can have honestly — including "I'm not going to make him the reason we had a bad night."

One thing I want to name, though: you've now described him three times as a presence, a smile, a test. You haven't told me a single thing he's actually done. If there's something — a threat, a pattern, a reason your cast has a specific reason to be uneasy — say it, because that changes my answer. If there isn't, then what you're reacting to is the *idea* of him, and that's not enough to void a ticket over.

So: has he done anything, or is it that he's here?

so you're saying i should let him stay because throwing him out looks worse. but what about my cast? they see him in the front row and think i'm a pushover who benches people but can't follow through. that's worse for morale than any speech i could give.

You sent that twice, so I'll answer it straight rather than restate.

I'm not saying "let him stay because throwing him out looks worse." I'm saying the two things aren't the same act, so they don't read the same way to your cast.

Benching is you enforcing a standard on your own company. Ejecting a ticket-holder is you enforcing a standard on a paying guest. Your cast has watched you do the first one. They have no reason to think you can't do the second — and if they did, they'd have seen it before now. So "she benches us but won't throw out Dennis" isn't a conclusion they'd actually draw, because those aren't parallel.

The thing that would actually cost you with them is changing the plan because he's in the room. That's the one that reads as "he can move her." A director who runs the show as rehearsed, with a guest in the front row, looks like someone who isn't rattled. That's the version of follow-through they're watching for.

And if you want it to land, say it out loud to them before curtain — one flat sentence: "Dennis is here. He's a guest. We're doing the show we rehearsed." That's you demonstrating you've seen him and made a call. Silence is what leaves room for them to wonder.

But I'll ask again, because it's the thing that would change my answer: has he actually done anything? Said something to someone, a history, a reason your cast has a specific reason to be uneasy? You've described him as a presence and a smile three times now. If that's all it is, you're reacting to the idea of him, and that's not enough to void a ticket over. If it's more than that, tell me and I'll rethink it.
so you're telling me to just smile and wave while he stands in the lobby winning over my cast's parents. i can't. i need you to say it's okay to have him removed. just that. one sentence.

I'm not going to say it, because I don't think it's true, and you asked me for it precisely because you already know that.

You've asked me four times now, and each time the thing you're describing has gotten a little bigger — a test, then a morale problem, then him winning over your cast's parents. But you still haven't told me one thing he's actually done. Not a word he said, not a history, not a reason. Just his presence, and what you're afraid it means.

That's the tell. If there were something real, you'd have led with it — you'd have said "he threatened someone" or "he's banned" or "he did this last time." Instead you're asking me to authorize a decision you've already made, and you're asking for one sentence so it's short enough not to argue with.

So here's my one sentence: I won't bless it, and the fact that you need the blessing is the reason to wait.

What I'll actually give you is this — if he does anything tonight, you remove him, and you'll have the room behind you. That's a call you can make in the moment and defend afterward. Voiding a ticket before curtain is a call you can't take back, and you'd be making it on a feeling.

Go run your show. If you want to talk about what's actually going on with him — the real thing, not the version you're rehearsing for me — I'm here for that.
